In the last few months, I have seen a dramatically increased interest in games which feature or are solely build around a co-op mode (that is, a mode where the player joins in with one or only a handful of friends rather than the 15+ person teams you'd usually find in online games).

Of course the phenomenon isn't entirely new, with games like Left for Dead, the ancient multiplayer mode for Bioware's Infinity Engine titles, or even just the old SNES/Playstation sidescrollers coming to mind. However, more recent games increasingly have slapped co-op modes onto genres where they previously were rather unusual (such as the single player campaigns for the RTS games Red Alert 3 and DoW II: Retribution allowing co-op gameplay), or have entirely have scrapped the game mechanics of the previous titles for the sake of co-op gameplay (Overlord: Fellowship of Evil and Fable: Legends).

Now, naturally people should be able to play the game however they damn well like, but I'm genuinely curious why gamers increasingly ask for such co-op features.

Is it related to the increasing cross-platform publishing and compability (with co-op having its roots in console gaming, imho)?

Is it some kind of social trend in the gaming community to play games with friends rather than going for a (perhaps more immersive) single-player experience?

Or is it (however unlikely) based on the rise of gaming e-celebs that get millions of views on their vids where they play co-op games with other e-celebs?
Where does the sudden surge in interest for co-op games/ co-op modes come from?
The time I spent on Chip & Dale wasn't wasted, those experiences are perfectly relative 25 years later.
I think it's a case of supply and demand. The supply of them has decreased over time, so people are demanding more. IMO anyways.

I think it is the natural Evolution of social gaming.

First there were PvP FPS games. People would band together, form clans and develop tactics.

Then there were open MMO's. you had everyone competing for the same resources, but in groups of friends.

Next they introduced instances to help all the competing resource issues. you would go in as a group and be the only one in there.

Finally, they realize that even within a guild, most people only hang with 6-10 people on a regular basis anyway, so why not capitalize on that concept.

I think the popularity of coop shows that many people enjoy playing games together, rather than against each other. I think overall there is also a gap in the market for good coop games, there are relatively few, compared to how many people like to play coop games.

When you play coop it doesn't matter, who is better at the game, you can help each other out and both have fun. In a competitive game the better player will have all the fun winning over and over, while the worse player gets frustrated by losing constantly. The better player might also get bored, since his opponent offers no challenge. It's more difficult to get real-life friends who you want to play games with on board for competitive games.

Here's my theory:

First there was local co-op and "take turns" games. When the internet became more affordable and common, online gaming brought the focus to online competitive multiplayer, so that anyone who owns a gaming system can play at home with a lobby full of people. Nowadays gaming itself is more common; it's fairly affordable, popular, and kids who grew up playing all have game systems. This is important because it means an era where anyone who plays online often has a few friends to play online with, which fuels the demand for co-op games to play together.

Competitive gaming is fun, but it was born in an era when you may have been the only one of your friends who had a game system and played online with it. Nowadays that's a lot more common.

Today I'm breaking in my new GeekVape Griffin with dual fused claptons wrapped around a 2.5mm bit, reading in at a really, really low (for me) 0.15 ohms. This thing is pretty amazing, like the Crius on Steroids. Way better top fill feature, much bigger deck, wicking was a breeze. So far, I've put the better part of five tanks through it and not one single drop of juice through the AFC, at any of the seams, at the top when filling etc. This thing is a beast and a half.

My only regret is having one mouth and one set of lungs, because now my Righteous Avocado (I've given it the appropriate surname, dubbed it if you will) sits cold and alone. I may just have to double fist this shit today.

Dang, GeekVape is knocking it out of the park this year on stuff.
That's interesting! I haven't heard of them prior to the other week when the Avocado was first brought to my attention. How is it? It looks like a kind of half-baked idea at first glance.

The Avocado or the Griffin?

The Avocado is running on the same idea that the Haze did - put a RDA deck on top of a tank with juice ports that let you stick a smidge of wick down into. As you vape, the cotton gets dry, but tipping the whole thing lets juice hit those holes and soak into the cotton. Like a Genesis-style Rebuildable without having to get into the SS mesh and whatnot. Smaller tank, so it's no big deal to tip 'n saturate. There's the option for dual coils, with dual wicking holes, but they provide a ceramic block that blocks off the juice holes on one side. Unlike the Haze, you can choose which side to build on and which side to block off. I, personally, do not like dual coil set ups in it. I tried it, it worked, but it wasn't... right. I like single coils. Better airflow, and some control on it (you can set up the airflow, like, a dozen different ways - as opposed to the Haze, which is one slot take it or leave it). Filling the tank by taking that ceramic block out first isn't nearly the PITA that I thought it was going to be. Lastly, instead of durable plastic, we've got some glass tanks (clear and a frosted one, so a backup woo!). Wide-bore drip tip with a standard DT adapter that sits flush as a honey bucket. I di-di-di-dig it. It's probably my favorite piece right now, my Righteous Avocado.

The Griffin is an RTA in the same style as the OBS Crius. Velocity-style deck, big ol' juice channels, wide-open airflow. I was in love with the Crius, and because of that love, I looked past a lot of stuff. Construction wasn't top-notch, I fucked mine up trying to separate parts to clean and it never did fully ... recover. It leaked, from the AFC and from the top fill section. The top fill was an awesome idea, but the execution left something to be desired - unless you were either using a perfect dripper or super patient with it, you were going to flood out and spill at least a drop on the outside of the tank. The Griffin borrowed the top fill idea from the Crown (take the whole top off, take it off baby!), and pretty much ran down the list of everything one could do to make the Crius sing - then did it, and called it the Griffin. No leaking, good seals. Easy to tear down and clean, easy to reassemble. Deck is much bigger than the Crius, easier to build on and you can get beefier coils in there. Wicking and juice control was fine IMO on the Crius, and bigger juice channels made moving up to the Griffin fairly easy. No. Leaks. I'm pretty happy with the lack of juice in my pocket and on my finger tips.
